Timeshare Scam UK: How to Spot and Avoid Holiday Property Traps

Timeshare scams promise the holiday of a lifetime but deliver decades of unwanted fees and legal entanglement.

By Alex Bacsa · Published 2026-07-03 · 8 min read

timeshare scam UKtimeshare fraudholiday property scamtimeshare exit scamfake timeshare investment
Key rule: verify through an official route you opened yourself, not the link, number, app, or payment details supplied by the suspicious message.

Being targeted right now? Do this

  1. Stop. Don’t pay, transfer money, or share passwords, PINs, or one-time codes.
  2. Contact your bank on the number on the back of your card if your money or details may be at risk.
  3. Report it — call Action Fraud on 0300 123 2040 (Police Scotland: 101), and forward scam texts to 7726.

What is a timeshare scam?

A timeshare scam tricks UK consumers into buying or 'investing' in fractional ownership of holiday properties, usually abroad. The scammer poses as a legitimate holiday club, property developer, or investment firm and uses high-pressure sales tactics, fake testimonials, and promises of cheap holidays or guaranteed returns to persuade victims to sign contracts. Once signed, victims discover the contract is binding, fees are far higher than promised, the property is not as advertised, and exit is nearly impossible without paying thousands more.

Some scams also target people already trapped in timeshare contracts, offering fake 'exit services' that charge upfront fees but deliver nothing. The core deception is that the victim believes they are making a sound financial decision or securing affordable holidays, when in reality they are entering a long-term financial commitment with little genuine benefit and no realistic way out.

Warning signs of a timeshare scam

  • **Unsolicited contact offering a 'free' holiday or prize**: You receive a call, email, or text claiming you have won a holiday or are eligible for a special offer. Legitimate holiday companies do not contact strangers this way.
  • **High-pressure sales tactics and urgency**: The seller insists you must decide immediately, claims the offer expires today, or says places are running out. Real investment decisions are never rushed.
  • **Vague or evasive answers about costs**: When you ask about total fees, annual charges, or exit terms, the seller changes the subject, minimises the figures, or says 'it depends'. Legitimate contracts are transparent upfront.
  • **Promises of guaranteed returns or easy resale**: The seller claims you will make money, that the property will appreciate, or that you can easily sell your share later. No investment is guaranteed, and timeshare resale is notoriously difficult.
  • **Request for upfront payment before you see a contract**: The seller asks for a deposit, 'booking fee', or 'registration fee' before providing written terms. Legitimate companies provide full documentation first.
  • **Property is overseas and difficult to visit**: The timeshare is in a remote location, a country with weak consumer protections, or a place you have never been. This makes it harder for you to verify the property or pursue complaints.
  • **Seller cannot provide independent references or verifiable company details**: When you try to check the company online, reviews are fake, the website is new, or contact details do not match official records.
  • **Contract is in a foreign language or uses confusing legal terms**: You are pressured to sign without understanding the full terms, or the contract is deliberately obscured.

How timeshare scams work: from first contact to the trap

The scam typically begins with an unsolicited phone call, email, or text offering a 'free' or heavily discounted holiday. The victim is invited to an 'information session' or 'presentation' at a hotel or resort, often abroad. At the venue, a high-pressure sales team uses emotional manipulation, fake testimonials, and manufactured urgency to persuade the victim to sign a contract. The victim is told they are buying a share in a luxury property, joining an exclusive holiday club, or making an investment that will pay dividends.

Once the contract is signed, the victim realises the true cost: annual maintenance fees are much higher than quoted, the property is not as advertised, booking is difficult or impossible, and the contract binds them for 10, 20, or even 40 years. When the victim tries to cancel or exit, they discover the contract is legally binding and exit fees are thousands of pounds. Some scammers then target the same victim again, offering a fake 'exit service' that charges upfront fees but delivers nothing.

By this point, the victim has lost thousands and is trapped in a contract they cannot escape.

How to verify if a timeshare offer is genuine

Before attending any presentation or signing anything, take these steps: (1) Search the company name online alongside 'scam', 'complaint', or 'review'. Look for patterns of negative feedback, especially from UK consumers. (2) Check the company's registration with Companies House (companieshouse.gov.uk). A legitimate UK business will have a verifiable company number and registered address. If the company is overseas, research its registration in that country. (3) Ask for the full contract in writing before any meeting or payment. A genuine company will provide this without hesitation.

Read it carefully or have a solicitor review it. (4) Contact Citizens Advice or Which? to see if they have published warnings about the company. (5) Call the property directly (not the number provided by the seller) and ask if the timeshare scheme is real and operating as described. (6) Be extremely wary of any company that cannot provide verifiable contact details, independent customer references, or a clear explanation of all costs in writing. If anything feels rushed, vague, or too good to be true, it almost certainly is.

What to do if you have already signed a timeshare contract

If you have signed a contract but have not yet paid, do not pay anything further. If you signed within the last 14 days, you may have a legal right to cancel under the Consumer Contracts Regulations. Check your contract for a cancellation clause and deadline. Write to the company immediately by registered post stating you wish to cancel and citing the 14-day cooling-off period. Keep a copy. If you have already paid and want to exit, do not use a third-party 'exit service' unless you have verified it independently — most are scams themselves.

Instead, contact a solicitor who specialises in timeshare law; many offer free initial consultations. Some timeshare companies will negotiate an exit for a fee, but always get independent legal advice first. If the company refuses to engage or the contract is genuinely unbreakable, you may need to accept the loss and stop paying (though this will damage your credit). Report the scam to Action Fraud and Citizens Advice so the pattern is recorded.

How to report a timeshare scam in the UK

Report the scam to Action Fraud by calling 0300 123 2040 or visiting actionfraud.police.uk. Provide as much detail as possible: the company name, contact details, dates of contact, what you were promised, and how much money (if any) you have lost. Action Fraud will log the report and may investigate if a pattern emerges. If you received the initial contact by email, forward it to the NCSC Suspicious Email Reporting Service at report@phishing.gov.uk. If you received a text message, forward it to 7726 (free). Contact Citizens Advice on 0808 223 1133 for free guidance on your rights and next steps.

If you have lost money, ask your bank about a chargeback or dispute if you paid by card. If the scammer is based overseas, your options are limited, but reporting still creates an official record. Consider also reporting to the FCA if the scam involved false investment claims (fca.org.uk). Keep all evidence: emails, texts, contracts, payment receipts, and notes of phone calls.

Frequently asked questions

I received a call saying I have won a free holiday or a timeshare prize. Is this genuine?

Almost certainly not. Legitimate companies do not contact strangers to offer unsolicited holidays or prizes. This is a classic opening move in a timeshare scam. Hang up, do not provide any personal details, and do not attend any presentation. If you are curious, search the company name online for complaints before engaging further.

I have already signed a timeshare contract and paid a deposit. Can I get my money back?

If you signed within the last 14 days, you may have a legal right to cancel under the Consumer Contracts Regulations. Write to the company immediately by registered post stating you wish to cancel. If more than 14 days have passed, your options are limited but not zero: contact a solicitor who specialises in timeshare law, ask your bank about a chargeback if you paid by card, and report the scam to Action Fraud. Do not pay any 'exit service' unless you have verified it independently.

What is the difference between a real timeshare and a timeshare scam?

Real timeshares are legal contracts that allow fractional ownership of a property. However, even legitimate timeshares are often poor value: fees are high, resale is difficult, and exit is costly. A scam timeshare uses deception to hide these facts, makes false promises about returns or resale value, uses high-pressure sales tactics, or targets people who are already trapped in a timeshare with a fake 'exit service'. If you are considering any timeshare, get independent legal advice first and never sign under pressure.

I have been offered a service to help me exit my timeshare contract. How do I know if it is a scam?

Many timeshare exit services are themselves scams. They charge upfront fees (often £1,000 to £5,000) but deliver nothing. Before paying, verify the company independently: search for complaints, check if they are registered with a professional body, and ask for references from people they have successfully helped. A legitimate solicitor will charge on a no-win-no-fee basis or provide a clear fee structure upfront. If a company pressures you to pay immediately or cannot provide verifiable references, avoid it.

Should I report a timeshare scam if I have not lost money yet?

Yes. Report it to Action Fraud (0300 123 2040) even if you have not paid. Your report helps police identify patterns and warn others. If you received contact by email or text, also report it to the NCSC (report@phishing.gov.uk) or 7726 respectively. The more reports that are filed, the more likely the scam will be investigated and shut down.
